question: What is the JUnit 5 test execution lifecycle?
title: JUnit 5 Test Lifecycle | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: The JUnit 5 lifecycle per class is: **`@BeforeAll`** once → then for **each** test method: **`@BeforeEach`** → **`@Test`** → **`@AfterEach`** → finally **`@AfterAll`** once. By default JUnit creates a **fresh test instance per method** (PER_METHOD), which is why `@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` must be `static`. This per-test reset is what keeps tests independent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the exact order and why fresh-instance-per-method enforces isolation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking one instance is reused across tests, or that @BeforeAll runs before each test
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect PER_METHOD default to test independence and to the static requirement on @BeforeAll

sections.title: The Execution Lifecycle
sections.content: JUnit 5 runs a predictable sequence around your tests. **`@BeforeAll`** runs **once** before any test in the class (static by default). Then, for **each** test method, JUnit: creates a **new instance** of the test class, runs all **`@BeforeEach`** methods, runs the **`@Test`**, then all **`@AfterEach`** methods. After every test has run, **`@AfterAll`** runs **once**. The default test-instance lifecycle is **PER_METHOD** — a fresh object per test — which guarantees no field state leaks between tests and is exactly why once-per-class hooks must be `static`.

sections.title: Lifecycle Order
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["@BeforeAll (static)
once per class"] --> B["new test instance"] B --> C["@BeforeEach"] C --> D["@Test method"] D --> E["@AfterEach"] E --> F{"more tests?"} F -->|yes| B F -->|no| G["@AfterAll (static)
once per class"] ```

sections.title: Observing the Order
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming one shared instance.** By default each test gets a new instance; a field mutated in one test is gone in the next.
- **`@BeforeAll` before each test.** It runs once, not per test — that's `@BeforeEach`.
- **Non-static `@BeforeAll`.** Fails to compile/run in the default PER_METHOD mode.
- **Relying on test order.** Methods aren't guaranteed to run top-to-bottom; never depend on it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Order** — `@BeforeAll` → (per test: `@BeforeEach` → `@Test` → `@AfterEach`) → `@AfterAll`.
- **PER_METHOD default** — fresh instance per test enforces isolation.
- **`@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll` static** — because no single instance owns them.
- **`@BeforeEach`** is the per-test reset point.
- **No order guarantee** between test methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The JUnit 5 lifecycle is a predictable sequence. First, BeforeAll runs once before any test in the class — it's static by default. Then, for each test method, JUnit creates a fresh instance of the test class, runs the BeforeEach methods, runs the actual Test method, and then runs the AfterEach methods. After all the tests have finished, AfterAll runs once. So the shape is BeforeAll once, then a repeating cycle of BeforeEach, test, AfterEach for every method, then AfterAll once.

The detail that ties it all together is the test instance lifecycle. By default it's per-method, which means JUnit creates a brand new object of the test class for every single test. That's deliberate — it guarantees that a field one test sets can't leak into another test, so tests stay independent. And that's exactly why BeforeAll and AfterAll have to be static: since there's no single instance that lives across all the tests, the once-per-class hooks belong at the class level.

The common misconceptions are thinking the same instance is reused across tests, or thinking BeforeAll runs before each test — it doesn't, that's BeforeEach. Another is assuming the test methods run in the order they're written; JUnit doesn't guarantee that, so I never write tests that depend on each other's order. To stand out, I'd connect the per-method default directly to test independence and to the static requirement on BeforeAll, because that shows I understand why the design is the way it is.

speakable_v2.hook: JUnit 5 creates a brand-new test class instance for each test by default. That's a deliberate choice to enforce isolation — and it's why @BeforeAll must be static.

beats.text: JUnit 5's default lifecycle is PER_METHOD: a new test class instance is created before every @Test method. The full order is @BeforeAll once, then for every test: @BeforeEach, @Test, @AfterEach, and finally @AfterAll once at the end.

By creating a fresh instance per test, JUnit makes it structurally impossible for instance fields to leak state between tests. You have to go out of your way to share state — which prevents accidental coupling.

items: @BeforeAll: static, runs once before any test in the class
@BeforeEach: runs before each @Test — fresh setup per test
@AfterAll: static, runs once after all tests in the class

beats.text: Because JUnit creates a new instance per test, @BeforeAll can't be an instance method — there's no 'one instance' to attach it to. So it must be static. If you annotate the class with @TestInstance(PER_CLASS), JUnit reuses one instance and @BeforeAll can be non-static. sharp edge: @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) risks tests sharing field state — be careful to reset in @BeforeEach.

items: Forgetting that @BeforeAll must be static in the default PER_METHOD lifecycle — it won't be called if it's not static
Assuming JUnit 4 behavior (single shared instance) — JUnit 5's PER_METHOD is a different default

speakable_v2.cap: The PER_METHOD lifecycle is JUnit 5's way of making test isolation the default, not something you have to manually maintain.
